title: AI Conquered Coding. Fast Food Is Next
gist: Voice AI in US fast-food drive-thrus is entering a second, quieter scaling wave after the viral failures of 2023–24: penetration has gone 4% (2024) to 5% (2025) to roughly 6% now, with Taco Bell at 890 lanes, 12% of White Castles running an agent named 'Julia', and McDonald's re-entering via a Google partnership after selling McD Tech Labs to IBM. The economic payoff so far is not labor substitution — headcount has held steady — but upselling: AI agents suggestive-sell 71% of the time versus a 58% industry average. (Despite its title, the article contains nothing about AI and coding; it is entirely about drive-thru voice AI.)

insights.claim: US fast-food voice-AI drive-thru penetration has risen from roughly 4 percent of locations in 2024 to 5 percent in 2025, with early research putting it at about 6 percent now, according to Intouch Insight's annual Drive Thru Survey.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Penetration is still single-digit — the addressable installed base for voice-AI vendors is ~94% untouched, so growth is ahead, not behind.
insights.quote: In 2024, roughly 4 percent of fast-food locations in the US used voice AI technology in the drive-thru lane, according to Intouch Insight’s annual Drive Thru Survey. Last year, that figure grew to 5 percent
insights.locator: The employee confirmed to Charpentier

insights.claim: Taco Bell announced in July 2026 that voice AI is live at 890 drive-thru lanes, more than 10 percent of its US locations, marking one of the largest single-chain deployments to date.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: A 10%+ single-chain rollout is the proof point vendors need to sell the rest of the franchise universe; watch Taco Bell same-store ticket disclosures for the first clean read on ROI.
insights.locator: Taco Bell announced in July

insights.claim: White Castle runs an AI ordering agent named 'Julia' at 12 percent of its locations and now opens every new restaurant with Julia taking orders by default, making AI ordering the standard build spec rather than a pilot.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: When AI ships in the standard new-store build, adoption compounds with unit growth automatically — a structurally different growth curve than retrofit pilots.
insights.quote: Twelve percent of White Castles use an AI named “Julia” in their drive-thrus; all new locations now open with Julia taking orders.
insights.locator: Twelve percent of White Castles

insights.claim: Chains that spent roughly three years quietly testing drive-thru voice AI are now judged technically ready and are expected to scale aggressively, per Intouch Insight's VP of sales and marketing.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: The industry insider view is that the S-curve knee is now — vendor revenue inflection should lead the penetration statistics by several quarters.
insights.quote: “They're going to start scaling this massively.”
insights.locator: The brands who have invested

insights.claim: Drive-thru voice AI followed a classic hype-disillusionment-recovery cycle: a 2019-2022 land grab, a 2023-2024 wave of viral failures and rollbacks, and a 2026 re-acceleration built on incremental fixes rather than a breakthrough model.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: A useful template for other physical-world AI deployments: the failure headlines mark the bottom, not the end — capital that exited at the trough missed the second wave.
insights.quote: AI drive-thru 1.0 was a flop, Schatzberg says.
insights.locator: Branded Hospitality recently partnered with Arc

themes.theme: Vendor churn and the McDonald's round trip

insights.claim: McDonald's started the drive-thru AI race in 2019 by acquiring startup Apprente into its McD Tech Labs division, then sold that unit to IBM, killed the technology outright, and as of summer 2026 is testing AI ordering again at five US locations in partnership with Google, in English and Spanish.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: The largest QSR buyer has now outsourced the AI stack to a hyperscaler rather than owning it — a template that shifts drive-thru AI spend toward cloud/model vendors instead of in-house labs.
insights.quote: McDonald’s eventually sold McD Tech Labs to IBM and later pulled the plug on the tech altogether.
insights.locator: Branded Hospitality sold off its early

insights.claim: The drive-thru voice AI supplier map is fragmented across Presto (Del Taco, Dairy Queen), SoundHound (Panda Express, White Castle), Nvidia and Omilia (Taco Bell), Google (McDonald's), and Arc (Jack's, Pollo Campero), with no single dominant platform.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Fragmentation plus a proven scaling thesis sets up a consolidation cycle; SoundHound is the pure-play public read on White Castle-style multi-year contracts.
insights.quote: Del Taco and Dairy Queen with Presto, Panda Express and White Castle with SoundHound, Taco Bell with Nvidia and Omilia.
insights.locator: McDonald’s kicked off the craze in 2019

insights.claim: Branded Hospitality, a food-service-technology investor, sold off its early AI-drive-thru positions during the 2023-24 disillusionment and has since re-entered by partnering with voice AI company Arc, whose customers include Jack's and Pollo Campero.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: A specialist investor round-tripping the same thesis signals that the second-generation vendors are materially different assets from the first — screen for who was funded post-2024, not pre-.
insights.quote: “Companies have evolved, technology has evolved, and they're like—we can fix a lot of those problems,”
insights.locator: Branded Hospitality recently partnered with Arc

insights.claim: Early AI drive-thru deployments destroyed value by creating remediation work for restaurant staff, prompting operators to demand a return to human headsets — the failure mode was operational overhead, not raw model quality.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: The buying criterion for enterprise AI in physical operations is net labor minutes saved, not accuracy benchmarks; vendors that cannot prove it churn out.
insights.quote: “The restaurants ended up spending more time smoothing over the problem they created,”
insights.locator: The restaurants ended up spending more time

insights.claim: AI drive-thru agents attempt suggestive selling on 71 percent of orders versus a 58 percent industry average, making incremental ticket size — not headcount reduction — the demonstrated economic payoff of the technology.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Model the ROI as a revenue-per-ticket uplift line, not a labor-cost line; that reframes the payback math and makes adoption attractive even at flat staffing.
insights.quote: Intouch Insight’s survey found that AI drive-thru agents use “suggestive selling”—upselling—71 percent of the time, compared to an industry average of 58 percent.
insights.locator: What chains are doing is using robots

insights.claim: Despite executive framing about efficiency, AI drive-thrus are not displacing fast-food jobs: White Castle's employment numbers stayed steady through its rollout and Taco Bell reports higher employee retention at voice-AI locations, because drive-thru workers multitask across roles that are extraordinarily hard to automate.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Cuts against the AI-jobs-apocalypse narrative for service labor; also means chains cannot underwrite these deployments on wage savings, so pricing pressure lands on vendors.
insights.quote: White Castle’s employment numbers have remained steady throughout the AI rollout. Taco Bell recently said that locations using voice AI have higher employee retention rates.
insights.locator: Executives claim that AI isn’t stealing anyone’s job

insights.claim: AI drive-thrus beat the industry average service time by 21 seconds per order according to Intouch Insight, the clearest quantified operational gain from the technology.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: At peak-hour throughput, 21 seconds per car is real capacity creation without capex on new lanes — the strongest quantified argument in the vendor pitch.
insights.quote: (Intouch Insight finds that, on average, AI drive-thrus beat the industry by 21 seconds.)
insights.locator: Four years into the White Castle’s partnership

insights.claim: AI order-takers underperform humans on both friendliness and order accuracy per Intouch Insight, and struggle with some accents and dialects, which chains patch by keeping a human employee on a headset ready to intervene.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: The human-in-the-loop fallback caps labor savings and is the hidden cost line in every deployment; watch for the quarter a chain claims it can drop the headset.
insights.quote: Intouch Insight found that AI drive-thrus tended to be less friendly than humans, with lower order accuracy.
insights.locator: The social media mockery was accompanied

insights.claim: Customer satisfaction with drive-thru voice AI is reported at 97 percent by Intouch Insight, far above what viral failure videos would imply and above the technology's own measured accuracy and friendliness scores.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Consumer backlash is not the binding constraint on adoption — unit economics and operational overhead are; discount the social-media risk premium.
insights.quote: Intouch Insight reported a whopping 97 percent satisfaction rate for the technology.
insights.locator: For customers like Reed, the uneasiness

insights.claim: Chick-fil-A, which consistently tops Intouch Insight's drive-thru friendliness ratings despite long lines, has never signaled any intent to replace human drive-thru workers with AI, and fast-growing coffee chains Dutch Bros and 7Brew have likewise rejected the technology.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: The service-premium brands are deliberately not adopting, which means AI drive-thru is a cost/throughput play for the value tier — a segmentation to respect when sizing the vendor TAM.
insights.quote: Chick-fil-A continually tops Intouch Insight’s ratings for friendliness at the drive-thru, despite its infamously long lines. The chain has never hinted at replacing a human worker with a robot.
insights.locator: Certain chains—especially those with a reputation

insights.claim: 7Brew's chief marketing officer explicitly frames human interaction as the product feature customers pay for, positioning refusal to automate as a competitive differentiator rather than a technology lag.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Expect 'human-served' to become an explicit marketing claim in consumer services, the way 'handmade' did in goods — a durable premium niche as automation spreads.
insights.quote: “For us, hospitality starts with genuine human connection, and that's something our guests consistently tell us they value.”
insights.locator: Every brand has to make choices

insights.claim: White Castle preserves an always-available option for customers to request a human worker, and credits its AI approach with contributing to employee satisfaction — it was the only fast-food chain in Fortune's top 20 best workplaces in retail last year.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: The operators winning with AI sell it internally as a worker-relief tool, not a replacement — a deployment playbook that reduces adoption friction across labor-sensitive industries.
insights.quote: White Castle was the only fast-food chain to crack Fortune’s top 20 list of best workplaces in retail last year

insights.claim: The next stage of drive-thru AI is data capture, not speech: systems that take orders in dozens of languages, recognize a customer's car on arrival, and generate offers from individual purchase histories — for example pushing a milkshake deal because a model computes the customer is 78 percent more likely to buy dessert on the second Tuesday of the month.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: The real asset being built is a per-customer QSR purchase graph — that, not order-taking, is where the durable margin and the regulatory risk both sit.
insights.quote: They can recognize a customer the moment their car pulls up to order. They could offer suggestions based on an encyclopedic knowledge of each customer.
insights.locator: The perceived benefits for fast-food chains

insights.claim: Operators deploying AI order-takers are consciously managing a privacy-perception ceiling on personalization, with White Castle's CMO summarizing the constraint as not wanting to seem creepy.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Self-imposed restraint, not regulation, is currently what caps the monetization of drive-thru customer data — a soft ceiling that competitors can break first.
insights.quote: “We never want to seem creepy,”
insights.locator: Imagine pulling up to McDonald’s

insights.claim: Consumer resistance to fast-food AI is framed around loss of social contact rather than order accuracy, with one customer describing relying on AI as eroding the ability to make community.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: The backlash vector for consumer AI is social, not functional — improving accuracy will not neutralize it, which matters for brands whose equity rests on warmth.
insights.quote: “I worry a lot about the ways that relying more and more on AI actually removes us from our human connections, like our ability to make community,”
insights.locator: When an automated voice began speaking

insights.claim: The pro-AI consumer case rests on consistency rather than quality: a former Dairy Queen drive-thru worker who encountered an AI order-taker argued that AI errors are more predictable than human errors and said she would have wanted an AI coworker.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Consistency is the consumer-facing selling point that survives imperfection — the same framing that will carry AI into other high-variance service roles.
insights.quote: But I think, as we've all seen with the advent of AI, there is more consistency with AI than there is in humans.
insights.locator: I think it's a great thing
